identity.title: Predictive Inverse Dynamics Models are Scalable Learners for Robotic Manipulation

problem.claim: Learn scalable policies for robotic manipulation across simulation and real-world settings.

contributions.claim: Introduces Predictive Inverse Dynamics Models (PIDM), an end-to-end paradigm that predicts actions from forecasted visual states, linking vision and action.
Implements PIDM as Seer, a Transformer-based model pretrained on large-scale robotic datasets and adaptable with limited fine-tuning data.
Reports strong performance and generalization across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish PIDM as an end-to-end approach that closes the loop between visual-state prediction and action prediction for scalable action learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that Seer significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in simulation and real-world experiments.
The authors report improvements of 13% on LIBERO-LONG, 22% on CALVIN ABC-D, and 43% on real-world tasks.
The authors report superior generalization to novel objects, lighting conditions, and environments under high-intensity disturbances.

narrative_sequence.summary: Scalable robotic-policy learning is described as mainly pursuing either action learning through behavior cloning or vision learning through large-scale visual pretraining.
The paper proposes PIDM, which predicts actions conditioned on forecasted robot visual states to connect vision and action end to end.
The practical model, Seer, uses Transformers for visual states and actions, with large-scale robotic pretraining and limited-data adaptation.
The authors report broad gains across benchmarks and real-world tasks, plus stronger generalization under varied objects, lighting, environments, and disturbances.
The authors state that code and models will be publicly available.

source_observation.claim: The abstract frames the method around an explicit vision–action feedback loop and reports benchmark-specific gains alongside generalization claims.

lessons.interpretation: A method’s central mechanism and its intended robustness targets can be presented together, making the claimed benefit traceable to the design.
lessons.application: When proposing a multimodal control method, state the cross-modal loop explicitly and pair each robustness claim with the relevant task or condition.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the method has no meaningful interaction between modalities or when the abstract lacks condition-specific evidence.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify baseline identities, evaluation metrics, statistical variation, or experimental protocols behind the reported percentage improvements.
The amount and composition of fine-tuning data, details of high-intensity disturbances, and the precise meaning of the real-world-task percentage are unspecified.

editorial_revisions.before: Code and models are stated to be publicly available.
editorial_revisions.after: The authors state that code and models will be publicly available.
